items.value: Light intensity in an ecosystem matters for animals as well as plants — the amber light both inhibited flowering in the plant and suppressed the aphid population that feeds on it
items.reasoning: The passage records two effects of the same light treatment: it inhibited flowering in a wild pea-family plant, and it significantly suppressed the number of pea-aphids because their food supply shrank. So the experiment shows the light regime reaching both a plant and an animal, which is exactly what option D states. Option A fails because the study never compared low with high intensity — only a low-intensity amber light is reported. Option C fails because the passage says nothing about white light aiding flowering; only the amber light's effect on flowering is described. Option B adds 'permanent', a claim about duration that the passage never makes.

items.value: Only assumptions 3 and 4 are valid — pollinators are scarce where natural vegetation is absent, and insect diversity underpins plant diversity
items.reasoning: Assumption 3 follows from the closing sentence: effective pollination requires resources such as refuges of pristine natural vegetation, so cultivated land stripped of natural vegetation will be poor in pollinators. Assumption 4 follows from the passage's core claim that about 80 percent of flowering plant species are animal-pollinated and that 'the reduction or loss of either affects the survival of both', making plant diversity dependent on insect diversity. Assumption 1 is invalid: the passage neither mentions India nor cereals, and it says only that at least one-third of crops depend on pollination, leaving the rest — which includes the wind-pollinated cereals — outside the claim. Assumption 2 is invalid because monoculture is never mentioned. Since 1 and 2 both fail, options A, B and C are all excluded and D is the only survivor.

items.value: Climate change makes water resources more critical to farmers while at the same time depleting them — more droughts drive groundwater use, while less recharge undermines the groundwater table
items.reasoning: The passage has two halves that meet in the middle. First, rising temperatures and fewer rainy days mean more run-off and less recharge, which threatens the groundwater table. Second, more frequent droughts have pushed farmers to depend more heavily on that same groundwater to save their crops. Option C is the only one that states both movements together, which is the crux. Option A misreads the regional climate models as the finding when they are only the method, and 'climate-smart agricultural practices' appear nowhere. Option B introduces dry-land cropping, which the passage never mentions. Option D captures only the last sentence and adds the evaluative words 'unsustainable' and 'risky', which the passage does not use.

items.value: Only assumptions 1 and 3 are valid — BPA may alter embryonic development in a living organism, and embryonic stem cells can model the physiological effects of pollutants
items.reasoning: Assumption 3 is precisely what the study did: mouse embryonic stem cells were used to detect and measure the toxicity of an environmental pollutant, so they served as a model for its physiological effects. Assumption 1 is valid because the passage already calls BPA a compound known to cause developmental abnormalities in humans, and the measured damage was to the specification of primary germ layers and neural progenitor cells — that is embryonic development, and the hedged word 'may' is all the passage needs to support. Assumption 2 fails on a single word: the researchers used the assays to detect and measure toxicity, never to find treatments, and no therapy is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

items.value: The remainder is 7
items.reasoning: The last digit of powers of 3 repeats in the four-step cycle 3, 9, 7, 1 (for exponents 1, 2, 3, 4), and the remainder on division by 10 is just that last digit. Dividing the exponent by 4 gives 2019 = 4 x 504 + 3, so the exponent sits at the third position of the cycle, the same place as 3 cubed = 27. Hence the last digit is 7 and the remainder is 7.

P occupies the thousands place, so the number equals 37981250369 + 1000P. Dividing the fixed part by 7 leaves a remainder of 6, and 1000 itself leaves a remainder of 6. The requirement is therefore 6 + 6P being a multiple of 7; since 6 is congruent to -1 modulo 7, this reduces to P being congruent to 6, and the only single digit that satisfies it is 6. Substituting back, 37981256369 divided by 7 is exactly 5425893767, confirming the value. Testing the other options: with P = 1, 7 or 9 the division leaves a non-zero remainder.

items.value: 20th May 2021 — the 140th day, when the frozen petrol price of Rs 90 equals the diesel price 69 + 0.15 x 140
items.reasoning: Equating the two formulas directly gives 80 + 0.1n = 69 + 0.15n, hence 0.05n = 11 and n = 220 — but the petrol formula is only valid up to m = 100, so this solution is outside its range and must be rejected. The catch is that from day 101 onward the petrol price is frozen at its day-100 value, 80 + 0.1 x 100 = Rs 90. Setting the diesel price equal to that gives 69 + 0.15n = 90, so 0.15n = 21 and n = 140, which is safely beyond day 100 and therefore valid. In the non-leap year 2021 the days run 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 = 120 through the end of April, so day 140 is 140 - 120 = the 20th of May.

items.value: P = 50 x 2 raised to the power n/12
items.reasoning: Doubling every 12 years means the number of doublings that have occurred after n years is n/12, and each doubling multiplies the population by 2, so the starting size of 50 is multiplied by 2 raised to the power n/12. Checking it: at n = 0 the formula gives 50, and at n = 12 it gives 50 x 2 = 100, correctly one doubling. Option C is wrong because 2 raised to 12n would double every year twelve times over — at n = 12 it would give 50 x 2 to the power 144. Options A and B describe straight-line growth by a fixed number of animals per year, not doubling.

items.value: 20% of the foreign students are boys
items.reasoning: Take the class as 100 students: 60 are Indian and 40 are foreign, and 50 in all are girls. Indian girls number 30% of 60 = 18, so the remaining girls, 50 - 18 = 32, must be foreign. That leaves 40 - 32 = 8 foreign boys, and 8 out of the 40 foreign students is 20%. The common trap is to report 8% — the share of boys in the whole class rather than among foreign students, which is what the question asks.

items.value: Neither conclusion follows — nothing links radios or mobiles to watches
items.reasoning: The only bridge to watches is 'Some computers are watches', and a particular premise like that tells us nothing about which computers are the watches. The computers that are watches could be entirely different computers from those that are mobiles, so Conclusion-II ('Certainly some mobiles are watches') does not follow. Conclusion-I is weaker still, since it needs both that link and the further step from radios through mobiles, and it fails for the same reason. Both conclusions are stated as certainties, and neither certainty can be established, so neither follows.

items.value: Assumptions 1, 3 and 4 are valid — fig trees act as keystone species, sacred trees aid biodiversity conservation, and fig trees help disperse the seeds of other trees
items.reasoning: Assumption 1 restates the definition of a keystone species using the passage's own words: in natural forests fig trees feed wildlife when other resources are scarce and support a high density and diversity of frugivores. Assumption 3 follows from the observation that sacred fig trees in disturbed sites may promote frugivore abundance, which is a conservation role. Assumption 4 follows from the last sentence, since seedlings of other tree species growing around fig trees imply that the frugivores visiting the figs are depositing those seeds there. Assumption 2 is the trap: the passage says other large trees are absent from agricultural and urban landscapes, but absence there is the result of human clearing — and of figs being spared as sacred — not evidence that other species cannot grow. Because 2 fails, options A and C are excluded.

items.value: Cover crops, mixed farming and polyculture (1, 4 and 5) are the practices compatible with agroecology as the passage describes it
items.reasoning: The passage defines agroecology by three tests: mimicking the biodiversity of natural ecosystems, closing nutrient loops by returning nutrients to the soil, and harnessing natural processes such as intercropping and integrating trees with livestock and crops. Cover crops build soil fertility and return organic matter to the soil; mixed farming is named almost verbatim in the passage's closing line; and polyculture is the biodiversity-mimicking, intercropping practice the passage praises. Fertigation delivers dissolved fertiliser through irrigation rather than recycling nutrients from the soil, so it does not close the loop the passage insists on. Hydroponics and vertical farming both grow crops without soil in controlled settings, which cannot satisfy a definition built on returning nutrients to the soil and mimicking natural ecosystems.

items.value: Computers are not completely safe — the passage's evidence is that networked devices, including those controlling cars and human bodies, are demonstrably hackable
items.reasoning: The passage builds to two claims: there is little evidence that the new generation of embedded gadgets will be more trustworthy than desktop computers, and hackers have already taken remote control of internet-connected cars and pacemakers. Both point at one inference — computers cannot be treated as safe — and option A is the only choice that states it. Option C misses the passage's opening move, which deliberately shifts attention away from abstract data towards physical objects and human bodies, so data security laws are not what the argument is about; it also prescribes a remedy the passage never raises. Option B blames the software companies, an attribution the passage never makes. The runner-up is option D: it would win if 'most critical inference' were read as 'what does this mean for the future', since the passage does forecast the arrival of the Internet of Things. But D says only that technology will 'affect our lives', which is true of any technology and drops the vulnerability that the whole passage is built on, so A is the sharper reading.

items.value: Only assumptions 4 and 5 are valid — micro-level interventions alone cannot bring down the infectious disease burden, and community hygiene through public health measures is what is really effective
items.reasoning: Assumption 4 comes straight from the Western Europe evidence: rates fell considerably only when general improvements in environmental conditions, clean water, sanitation and food security accompanied personal hygiene, so personal cleanliness on its own is not sufficient. Assumption 5 is the same point stated positively and matches the passage's opening claim that the risk of infectious disease is generated by a social and physical environment of poverty and insanitary conditions. Assumption 1 fails because the passage never says the hygiene-obsessed neglect community hygiene. Assumption 2 is the reverse of the passage, which links the obsession with hand hygiene to the emergence of resistant germs rather than to preventing them. The runner-up is option B, which swaps assumption 5 for assumption 3. Assumption 3 would win if 'a false sense of security' plus the marginalised emergence of resistant germs were read as a direct increase in infectious disease risk, and if assumption 5's phrasing were read as an exclusivity claim the passage contradicts when it says 'along with personal hygiene'. Assumption 3 is rejected here because the passage's charge against the market is a false sense of security and an ecological cost, never a measured rise in infection.

items.value: Both conclusions follow — some almirahs are certainly tables, and it is possible that some cats are not chairs
items.reasoning: Conclusion-I is a definite conclusion and it holds: some almirahs are chairs, and since all chairs are tables, those particular almirahs are tables, so 'some almirahs are tables' is certain. Conclusion-II is phrased as a possibility, and the test for a possibility conclusion is whether the case can be arranged consistently with the premises. It can: nothing in the three statements forces any cat to be a chair — the cats that are almirahs need not be among the almirahs that are chairs — so a diagram in which no cat is a chair is entirely consistent, and 'some cats may not be chairs' follows. Note the deliberate contrast in wording: Conclusion-I says 'Certainly' while Conclusion-II says 'may', which signals that the two are being tested by different standards. The runner-up is option A (only Conclusion-I). It would win under a stricter convention in which possibility conclusions are not entertained at all and every conclusion must be established as definite — under that reading Conclusion-II would be rejected because it is not certain that any cat fails to be a chair (all cats could be chairs without contradicting the premises).

items.value: The ball hits the ground 6 times
items.reasoning: Starting at 1.5 m = 150 cm and taking four-fifths each time, the successive heights from which the ball falls are 150, 120, 96, 76.8, 61.44 and 49.152 cm. Each of those falls ends in one strike on the ground, so counting the heights counts the hits. The stopping rule bites on the last one: the ball falls from 49.152 cm and hits the ground — that is the sixth hit — but because this previous height is below 50 cm it does not bounce again. The heights 61.44 and above are all at least 50 cm, so every earlier strike is followed by a bounce, giving six hits in total.

items.value: 14 consonants have mirror images that differ from the original shape
items.reasoning: A capital letter looks unchanged in a mirror exactly when it has a vertical axis of symmetry. The letters with such an axis are A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X and Y. Removing the vowels A, E, I, O and U leaves 21 consonants, of which the symmetric ones are H, M, T, V, W, X and Y — seven letters. The remaining 21 - 7 = 14 consonants (B, C, D, F, G, J, K, L, N, P, Q, R, S, Z) reverse in a mirror and so do not look like their original shapes.

items.value: 25 km — the bank lies due east of the house
items.reasoning: Track the turns from the house: driving 10 km south puts her 10 km below the start. Facing south, a left turn points east, so 20 km takes her 20 km east. Facing east, a left turn points north, so 40 km carries her from 10 km south to 30 km north. Facing north, a right turn points east, so 5 km takes her to 25 km east. Facing east, a right turn points south, so the final 30 km brings her back from 30 km north to the latitude of the house. She therefore ends 25 km east and 0 km north of the start, and the shortest distance is simply 25 km.

Only 700 to 999 need checking, since 1000 has a digit sum of 1. With a hundreds digit of 7 the other two digits must sum to 3, giving the four numbers 703, 712, 721 and 730. With a hundreds digit of 8 they must sum to 2, giving 802, 811 and 820. With a hundreds digit of 9 they must sum to 1, giving 901 and 910. That is 4 + 3 + 2 = 9 integers in all.

items.value: An angle less than 45 degrees north of east — she is 8 km east and 6 km north of the start, about 37 degrees north of east
items.reasoning: The 12 km north and 6 km south partly cancel, leaving a net displacement of 6 km north, and the last leg adds 8 km east. So relative to her starting point she is 8 km east and 6 km north, which is a direction north of east — this rules out the two 'south of east' options. Because the eastward distance (8 km) exceeds the northward distance (6 km), the direction leans more towards east than north, so the angle measured from east towards north is under 45 degrees; precisely, the angle whose tangent is 6/8 = 0.75, about 37 degrees.
